title: delete arr[i] leaves holes
description: `delete arr[i]` does not shift later elements or shrink `length` — it leaves a sparse hole where the slot reads as `undefined`, and most array methods silently skip it. Use `splice` (mutate) or `filter` (new array) to actually remove an element.

notes: `delete arr[i]` was inherited from object-property semantics — on arrays it almost never does what you want.
Length is unchanged after `delete`, so loops over `arr.length` still visit the hole (as `undefined`).
`JSON.stringify` serializes holes as `null` — that's why `[1, , 3]` prints as `[1,null,3]` in the runner.
Iteration methods are split: `forEach`, `map` (preserves but doesn't invoke the callback), `filter`, `reduce`, `some`, `every` SKIP holes; index-based `for` and `for...of` VISIT them.
`Array.from(arr)` and the spread `[...arr]` MATERIALIZE holes into real `undefined` slots — useful when you need consistent iteration.
To actually remove by index, use `arr.splice(i, 1)` (mutates, returns the removed slice) or `arr.filter((_, j) => j !== i)` (new array).

questions.q: After `const a = [1, 2, 3]; delete a[1];`, what is `a.length`?
questions.explain: `delete` clears the slot but does not change `length` — the array is now sparse but still reports length 3.

questions.q: After `const a = [1, 2, 3]; delete a[1];`, what does `a[1]` evaluate to?
questions.explain: Reading a hole returns `undefined` — same as reading any unset property on an object.

questions.q: Which expression removes the element at index 1 AND shifts later elements down?
questions.explain: `splice(1, 1)` removes one element at index 1 and shifts the rest left, decrementing length. The other three leave the array in a broken state.

questions.q: After `const a = [1, 2, 3]; delete a[1];`, how many times does `a.forEach(fn)` call `fn`?
questions.explain: `forEach`, `map` (callback), `filter`, and `reduce` all silently skip holes. That's why `delete` produces hard-to-spot bugs — the count is just off by one.

hints: `delete arr[i]` is the trap this lesson is about — don't reach for it.
`splice(i, 1)` mutates the array, removing 1 element at index `i` and shifting later elements left.
`splice` returns the REMOVED slice, not the mutated array — return `arr` directly.
